analysis.title: Goldman Warns Of Massive Oil Glut In 2027 As Gulf Barrels Flood Back Around Hormuz
key_insights: Goldman's 2027 Oil Analyst outlook ('Adaptation', Daan Struyven) has a base-case 2027 surplus of 2mb/d (production minus end-use demand), even with non-Gulf output growth slowing from 1.3mb/d in 2026 to flat in 2027 and a 1mb/d supply disruption allowance.

Goldman's base case has Brent averaging $88/bbl in 2027 and easing to $78/bbl by December 2027. Brent fair value falls from $90/bbl today to the high $70s by end-2027. WTI averages $78 and ends 2027 at $70.

Goldman calls 2026 a 'double major surprise': Hormuz was effectively closed far longer than expected, and prices rose less than the disruption implied. Global inventories fell only ~600mb (about 5% of stocks, 2.4mb/d) between March and October.

Goldman's ledger for the ~2,050mb of lost Gulf output: ~300mb from the 2025 pre-war surplus, ~775mb from demand destruction (especially China's switch to power and coal), ~375mb from stronger non-Gulf output (especially Brazil). Pipeline rerouting, dark exports, US Navy escorts and ship-to-ship transfers covered much of the remainder.

Goldman estimates the global liquids balance swung from a 0.6mb/d deficit in September to a 1.6mb/d surplus in October, driven by a 2mb/d month-over-month jump in Gulf crude exports to 100% of 2025 levels. The IEA estimates a 2mb/d October surplus and JPMorgan about 1.4mb/d.

Goldman expects Gulf liquids output to rise nearly 4mb/d from October over 2027, ending the year 1.4mb/d above the 2025 average, mostly from Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Iran's crude output is forecast to rise from 1.9mb/d in Q4 2026 to 2.9mb/d by Q4 2027.

Goldman expects 3.8mb/d of additional Hormuz-bypass pipeline capacity within a year (UAE West-East pipeline, a repurposed Saudi gas pipeline, Yanbu port expansion). With Iraq's Basra-Haditha project in 2028, Gulf exports via bypass pipelines could exceed 14mb/d, around 60% of 2025 export volumes, by end-2027.

Goldman assumes demand recovers to its pre-war trend everywhere except China. Persistent weakness in Chinese gasoline and diesel accounts for all of the 0.4mb/d permanent demand scarring by Q4 2027. Goldman now estimates China's total oil demand peaked in 2025.

Goldman's 2027 Brent forecast of $88 is $7 above the futures curve ($81 average for the nearby contract), and its monthly path is above the forwards through December 2027. The market already prices more glut than Goldman does.

Goldman estimates the Brent war premium fell from $27 on the Friday before the midterms to a few dollars last week, and says the crude risk premium 'appears quite low relative to the still significant geopolitical risks'. Hedge funds dumped $6.6 billion of Brent as the premium collapsed.

The glut is in crude only. Goldman expects US wholesale diesel to average $150/bbl in 2027, with US wholesale margins versus Brent averaging $59/bbl for diesel and $28/bbl for gasoline, against $28 and $18 in 2025.

Product tightness drivers: structural refining tightness (net global capacity growth of 0.4mb/d in 2027 and 0.3mb/d in 2028), Gulf product exports ~60% below 2025 levels, and Russian seaborne product exports 1mb/d below seasonal norms in October. Global refinery runs undershoot trend by 2.8mb/d in 2026 and 1.3mb/d in 2027.
The IEA said diesel remains the market's 'biggest concern', with members accelerating release of about 20 million barrels of diesel from emergency stocks.
Goldman sees US retail gasoline at $3.7/gal by end-2027 (from $4.0) and diesel at $4.6/gal (from $6.1).

Risks are two-sided. Upside: Brent could reach $130 and average about $120 in 2027 if Gulf output stays 2.7mb/d below 2025, with US wholesale diesel at $230/bbl and gasoline at $170 if another 3mb/d of refining is lost. Downside: Brent could fall into the $60s if Gulf output runs 2.6mb/d above 2025 and the 1mb/d disruption allowance never materializes.

Goldman's trade recommendations lean toward cheap upside: investors stay long summer 2027 European gasoline, fast-money traders lean against big swings in the risk premium, producers buy puts or collars, and refiners lock in deferred diesel margins from late 2027.

The ZeroHedge author adds their own view (not Goldman's) that the asymmetry points up for the next few months, given a near-zero risk premium, Goldman's forecast being above the curve, and diesel at $150.

Products stay tight on refining constraints, damaged Gulf refineries and Russian export limits. US wholesale diesel is forecast to average $150/bbl in 2027.

risk_factors: Renewed Mideast escalation involving attacks on energy infrastructure could push Brent to $130.
Hormuz bypass pipelines are exposed to Iranian threats.
The longer the US-Iran standoff lasts without a deal, the higher the odds of Iranian escalation.
Refinery maintenance postponed into spring 2027 already exceeds seasonal norms by 1mb/d, a risk to product supply.
Freight has upside risks. Crude and product freight is seen easing to $9/bbl by end-2027 from $15 today.
Goldman's fair-value model change added about $13 to Brent fair value (from $77 to just over $90).
vol_and_positioning: Hedge funds dumped $6.6 billion of Brent as the midterms removed the war premium.
Producers are advised to buy puts while put skew is low, or collars since call vol remains high.
Goldman says fast-money traders should prefer long positions when the risk premium is small or negative, and notes it is small now.
Refiners are advised to lock in deferred diesel margins from late 2027, which still embed a 'very high market risk premium'.
Dated Brent slipped below the nearby futures contract, per Morgan Stanley (via Reuters), a sign of a soft physical market.
geopolitical: Strait of Hormuz has been effectively shut for most of 2026 during the Iran war, with the IRGC still reportedly seeding it with mines.
US blockade of Iran continues. Goldman's Iran output forecast blends the blockade continuing with it being lifted.
A sustainable US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough is expected to remain challenging, especially on governance of the Strait and sequencing of mutual concessions.
Iran has openly threatened to hit Gulf bypass pipelines.
Ukraine's drone campaign is assumed to keep Russian seaborne product exports constrained.
Polymarket odds of Hormuz traffic normalizing by year-end fell from roughly 90% in June to mid-single digits.
cross_bank_references: JPMorgan pegged the October surplus at about 1.4mb/d.
Morgan Stanley flagged that Dated Brent slipped below the nearby futures contract, according to Reuters.
Goldman's 2027 Gulf supply view is 'a touch more bullish' than the 1.1mb/d in Sunday's flagship commodity outlook.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's forecast is above the futures curve, the risk premium is down to a few dollars, diesel is at $150, and escalation could take Brent to $130. Goldman's trades lean toward cheap upside.
tension_points.bear_case: Gulf exports are back at 100% of 2025 levels, bypass pipelines add 3.8mb/d, China's demand has peaked, and a 2mb/d surplus takes Brent to the high $70s by end-2027, or the $60s if no disruption occurs.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sustainable US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough would remove the upside tail. Renewed attacks on energy infrastructure, or Gulf output staying 2.7mb/d below 2025, would invalidate the glut thesis.

theme_stances.key_argument: Gulf exports recovering, bypass pipelines and peaked Chinese demand produce a 2mb/d surplus in 2027.
theme_stances.evidence: the world has learned to live with a closed Hormuz a little too well

theme_stances.key_argument: Refining capacity, Gulf product export losses and Russian constraints keep diesel and gasoline tight despite the crude glut.
